title: How mangroves protect the coast
text:
Along many tropical coastlines, where the land meets the sea, there are forests that stand in salt water for part of every day. These are mangrove forests. Indonesia has more mangroves than any other country in the world, and they do important work for people and for wildlife.

Living in salty, muddy water is difficult for most plants, but mangroves have clever ways to survive. Some kinds take in salty water and push the extra salt out through their leaves, where you can sometimes see it as tiny white crystals. Others stop most of the salt from entering their roots. The thick mud contains very little air, so many mangroves grow special roots that poke up out of the mud like pencils. These roots take in air when the tide is low.

The most important job mangroves do is protecting the shore. Their tangled roots act like a natural wall. When waves roll in, they lose energy as they push through the roots, so they reach the land more gently. This means that less soil is washed away, and villages behind the mangroves are safer during storms.

The roots also trap mud and sand carried in by the water. Slowly, layer by layer, this builds up the land and helps to keep the coastline in place.

Mangroves are nurseries for sea life too. Young fish, crabs and prawns hide among the roots, where large hunters cannot easily reach them. When they are bigger, many swim out to the open sea. As a result, fishing families who live nearby often have better catches.

Finally, mangroves help the whole planet. They take in carbon dioxide from the air and store large amounts of carbon in their roots and in the mud below them.

Sadly, many mangrove forests have been cleared to make space for buildings and fish ponds. Because of this, planting and protecting mangroves is now an important task for coastal communities.
